chunks: From him, from Uyaynah, the seller of reeds, from Ibrahim ibn Maymun, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'We travel to Ahwaz on ships, so we combine the prayer in them.' He said, 'Yes, there is no harm in that.' I said, 'And we prostrate on what is in them and on the pitch (tar)?' He said, 'There is no harm.'

key_terms.السُّفُنِ: Ships, referring to the vessels used for river travel on the Shatt al-Arab.
key_terms.الْأَهْوَازِ: Ahwaz, a city in Khuzestan, Iraq, often referenced in early Shia narrations as a destination for travel.
key_terms.الْقِيرِ: Pitch or tar, a substance used to seal ships, here discussed regarding its ritual purity for prostration.
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِهِ بَأْسٌ: There is no harm in it, a common juristic phrase indicating permissibility (jawaaz) without strict obligation or prohibition.

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray and prostrate on the deck or pitch of a ship according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the practicalities of prayer aboard ships, permitting the combination of prayers during the journey and validating prostration on the ship's deck or its pitch (qir) covering. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle of ease (*taysir*) in travel, acknowledging that the structural materials of a vessel do not invalidate the purity required for *sujud*. It highlights the flexibility of ritual practice when facing the constraints of movement and limited space during maritime travel.
